common.siteDescription: We all write code. What's your type? Explore your preferences in control, constraints, cognition, and values.

home.title: We all write code. What's your type?
home.description: BUGTI is a programmer personality test about coding preferences. Discover how you like to write code and what drives your choices.
home.dimensionsDescription: Control, constraints, cognition, and values describe four trade-offs behind your technical choices. Explore each preference pair to understand what shapes your coding habits.
home.personalitiesDescription: Four dimensions combine into 16 approaches to code. From the Philosopher to the Doer, meet familiar characters and explore how different programmers think and act.

dimensionsPage.title: Four trade-offs. Your coding preferences.
dimensionsPage.description: Explore control, constraints, cognition, and values. Each dimension describes two valid preferences; the four letters combine into a personality type.
dimensionsPage.pairsLabel: Four preference pairs in order: C/D, F/G, R/E, U/A

test.title: How do you like to write code?
test.description: 32 everyday coding decisions. Answer based on your own preferences.
test.instructionExperience: Imagine facing each situation and choose how you would prefer to act, even if it has never happened to you. Assume you can carry out either approach.
test.instructionChoice: Assume you have a reasonable choice and time to decide. Both approaches must meet necessary correctness, security, compliance, and reliability requirements.
test.instructionHonesty: Answer for yourself, not your team’s mandatory rules. There are no right answers or better preferences.
test.instructionNeutral: Choose Neutral when you understand the scenario but have no overall preference. It is a scored answer, not a skip option.
test.limitation: For self-reflection. Not scientifically validated; not an assessment of engineering ability.
test.reviewDescription: You can change any answer before viewing your result.
test.resumeNotice: Your unfinished answers are saved in this browser tab.
test.storageUnavailable: Draft saving is unavailable. Your answers remain available until you reload or close this page.
test.leaveDescription: Your answers stay in this tab. You can come back to continue.
test.linkInvalid: The answers in this link could not be restored. Start a new test instead.

result.title: No result in this link
result.description: Complete the test to generate a result link you can save and reopen.
result.invalidDescription: The link may be incomplete or use an unsupported version. Copy the full original link or take the test again.
result.scoreExplanation: Scores summarize these answers on a 0–100 response index. They are not probabilities, rankings, or ability ratings.
result.balancedTitle: Your preferences do not resolve to one type
result.balancedDescription: At least one dimension is exactly balanced. Your complete dimensions still describe your choices.
result.incompleteDescription: Earlier “Cannot judge” responses leave affected dimensions unscored. Take the current test for a complete set of hypothetical choices.
result.nearBoundaryHelp: A different answer could shift this direction. Treat the type as a summary of these responses.
result.copyFailed: Copy manually from the field below.
result.shareDescription: The link contains your answers. Anyone with it can read them; the encoded query may also appear in server logs.
result.localLink: This address is local to your computer. Other people can use the link only after the site is deployed at an accessible address.
result.candidatesTitle: Types compatible with your balanced dimensions
result.allBalanced: All four dimensions are balanced. There is no overall directional tilt to assign a type.
result.patternBoth: You endorsed approaches on both sides on average.
result.patternNeither: You disagreed with approaches on both sides on average.
result.patternNeutral: Neither side has an average agreement direction.
result.patternNote: This response pattern can reflect different situations; it does not establish an inconsistent personality.
result.limitation: A reflection on your responses, not a scientifically validated assessment. Preferences can change with context and experience.
result.legacyNotice: This is an earlier questionnaire result. It keeps the original statements and scores. Take the current test to answer hypothetical situations.

about.purpose: Programmers can give different answers to the same technical problem. BUGTI explores the trade-offs behind those answers: who holds control, how much freedom to keep, how judgments are formed, and what is worth investing in.
about.limits: Projects, teams, and experience shape your choices. Use your four-letter type to reflect on your coding habits and discuss trade-offs with others.

error.notFoundDescription: The link may be incorrect. You can return to the BUGTI home page.
error.unavailableDescription: Return to the home page and try again. If the issue continues, please try later.

constraints.title: Constraints
constraints.question: Freedom of expression or upfront guarantees?

values.title: Values
values.question: What makes code worth investing in?

cognition.title: Cognition
cognition.question: Where does a technical judgment begin?

C.label: Control
C.description: Keep mechanisms visible, explainable, and adjustable, accepting complexity in exchange for control.

D.label: Delegation
D.description: Trust languages, frameworks, and platforms, saving effort for the problems that truly need you.

F.label: Flexibility
F.description: Keep room to combine and change things, accepting that developers will judge and verify some rules.

G.label: Guarantees
G.description: Encode rules in types and models to make invalid states harder to create.

U.label: Utility
U.description: Focus on benefits, costs, and maintenance. Extra investment needs a practical return.

A.label: Aesthetics
A.description: Value coherent structure and elegant expression, investing in the quality of the code itself.

R.label: Reasoning
R.description: Build a model first, using premises, causes, and boundaries to deduce why a solution works.

E.label: Experimentation
E.description: Start with prototypes, measurements, and observations, then revise judgments using actual results.

typesPage.title: 16 personalities. 16 ways to approach code.
typesPage.description: Some ask why first. Others start by trying. Explore these familiar characters and see which feels like you when you write code.
typesPage.codeOrder: Four letters, four questions in order
typesPage.grouping: Start with Control (C) or Delegation (D). C splits by Reasoning (R) or Experimentation (E); D splits by Flexibility (F) or Guarantees (G). CR/CE use the first and third letters of the type code; DF/DG use the first two.

CR.title: Planners
CR.description: Keep key mechanisms in your hands and think through principles, boundaries, and structure first. Understand why an approach works, then put your judgment into the system.

CE.title: Practitioners
CE.description: Keep critical parts adjustable and build judgment by working with them directly. Try, verify, and refine, letting actual feedback guide the next step.

DF.title: Pioneers
DF.description: Use existing capabilities while keeping your route open. Choose, combine, or replace tools to find an approach that fits the goal and explore new possibilities.

DG.title: Guardians
DG.description: Delegate general complexity to mature tools and rely on clear rules and guarantees. Let systems handle repetitive details so the parts work together reliably.

CFRU.name: Philosopher
CFRU.summary: Understand why first, then find a solution that makes sense and works.
CFRU.description: You tend to ask why first. You want to understand the key mechanisms before finding a way to solve the problem. Languages and techniques can vary, but the solution must make sense. Understanding principles helps you rely less on guesswork and keep more control.
CFRU.inPractice: You may trace a mechanism, outline an approach, then change only the parts needed for the goal.
CFRU.watchFor: A convincing model can still omit a real-world condition. Use small checks to challenge the assumptions.
CFRU.collaboration: Share the assumptions behind your choice, and ask a hands-on teammate to identify a useful first experiment.

CFRA.name: Artist
CFRA.summary: Master the mechanisms so your code can express your own ideas.
CFRA.description: You see programming as a way to express ideas. You want to understand the mechanisms and have enough freedom to organize code in your own way. Even after the feature works, you still care about precise expression, elegant structure, and whether the work reflects your intent.
CFRA.inPractice: You may design your own composition and refine the concepts until the implementation expresses your intent.
CFRA.watchFor: Personal expression can become costly for other maintainers. Check whether another person can follow the structure.
CFRA.collaboration: Explain the idea behind the design and agree on which refinements are worth the shared time.

CFEU.name: Engineer
CFEU.summary: Adjust what you need and judge the tool by what it actually does.
CFEU.description: You treat programming as a tool for solving problems. You make changes when needed, try them in practice, and prefer to adjust the critical parts yourself. What matters is whether the tool meets the need. Once the problem is solved, you usually do not invest more just for the code's sake.
CFEU.inPractice: You may inspect a problem, try a local change, and keep the solution that demonstrably meets the need.
CFEU.watchFor: A local fix can leave wider interactions unexplored. Test the adjacent behavior before calling the task done.
CFEU.collaboration: Offer a reproducible example and a clear outcome, then invite review of the change boundary.

CFEA.name: Inventor
CFEA.summary: Try new possibilities yourself and build something clever that feels right.
CFEA.description: You enjoy trying things yourself and turning ideas into something that runs. An existing implementation is rarely the end: you wonder how else it could be changed or combined. You enjoy the discoveries in experimentation and want the result to feel fresh, clever, and true to your idea.
CFEA.inPractice: You may experiment with mechanisms you can change and use discoveries to create a distinctive implementation.
CFEA.watchFor: Repeated experimentation can expand the task. Define when to stop exploring and choose an approach.
CFEA.collaboration: Show an early prototype and separate essential discoveries from optional refinements.

CGRU.name: Goalkeeper
CGRU.summary: Understand the boundaries and stop avoidable problems before they happen.
CGRU.description: You care about what may happen and what must be prevented. You think through the boundaries, then put the key rules into the parts you can control. You are willing to prepare more so the system has fewer surprises and problems are easier to handle when they arise.
CGRU.inPractice: You may map failure paths and encode key boundaries in code you directly maintain.
CGRU.watchFor: Preparing for every hypothetical failure can cost more than its benefit. Prioritize plausible, consequential cases.
CGRU.collaboration: Explain the risks each rule addresses and agree on which safeguards are necessary now.

CGRA.name: Architect
CGRA.summary: Give every concept a place and every rule a reason in a coherent whole.
CGRA.description: You want the system to have a clear, consistent structure. You want control over key mechanisms, a precise place for each concept, and a reason for every rule. Even when the system runs, ambiguity, duplication, and contradictions make you want to reorganize the design.
CGRA.inPractice: You may align the model, interfaces, and implementation so each concept has an explicit place.
CGRA.watchFor: A coherent structure may need several changes before a feature ships. Set a useful stopping point for the design.
CGRA.collaboration: Make the model visible and discuss which consistency rules are essential versus optional.

CGEU.name: Inspector
CGEU.summary: A guarantee still needs a hands-on check before you trust it.
CGEU.description: You like explicit guarantees and habitually check whether they hold. You test boundaries, observe behavior, and adjust critical details to see whether the system works as expected under real conditions. For you, it should be fine needs to become I tried it and it is fine.
CGEU.inPractice: You may test explicit constraints and adjust the mechanisms where observations reveal a gap.
CGEU.watchFor: Passing checks cover the tested cases. Revisit assumptions when the surrounding system changes.
CGEU.collaboration: Share the boundary cases and distinguish observed behavior from guarantees not yet tested.

CGEA.name: Craftsperson
CGEA.summary: Verify and refine by hand until correct work also feels well made.
CGEA.description: You want things to follow clear rules and every detail to be well considered. You like hands-on verification and repeated adjustment, continuing to refine after correctness is established. Accurate behavior, coherent structure, and clean expression are worth a little more time.
CGEA.inPractice: You may repeatedly verify and refine an implementation so its behavior and expression fit together.
CGEA.watchFor: Refinement can continue after the practical need is met. Agree on a finish line for the current iteration.
CGEA.collaboration: Use concrete examples in review and separate correctness fixes from craftsmanship improvements.

DFRU.name: Planner
DFRU.summary: Work out the approach first, then use tools where they make effort count.
DFRU.description: You think through the goal and approach before deciding which tools to use. You do not want to take on work that existing capabilities can handle, and you adapt the implementation route as needed. You care about arranging your effort so it solves the problems that really matter.
DFRU.inPractice: You may compare approaches on paper, then compose existing tools around the actual goal.
DFRU.watchFor: A tool can fit the plan but hide an assumption. Check the contract before delegating the mechanism.
DFRU.collaboration: Explain why each tool belongs in the plan and keep replacement boundaries clear.

DFRA.name: Director
DFRA.summary: Start with a vision and bring different tools together to express it.
DFRA.description: You like forming an overall idea, then bringing suitable tools and modules together. You do not need to handle every low-level detail yourself, but you want those capabilities to express your design accurately. You care about how the parts connect and whether the whole is clear and coherent.
DFRA.inPractice: You may begin with an overall idea and organize existing capabilities into a coherent expression.
DFRA.watchFor: The desired composition may differ from what a tool supports. Verify important extension points early.
DFRA.collaboration: Share the intended whole, then invite feedback on the connections between parts.

DFEU.name: Doer
DFEU.summary: Try what works, change what doesn't, and focus on getting it done.
DFEU.description: You first ask whether the problem has been solved. You use what is available, try whichever approach works, and switch when it does not. You have little attachment to languages or technical routes and do not want complexity without a practical return. Getting it done is your most direct measure.
DFEU.inPractice: You may start with available tools, test a direct route, and change it when it stops serving the goal.
DFEU.watchFor: Frequent route changes can leave implicit assumptions. Record the choices future maintainers need.
DFEU.collaboration: Show what works, explain what remains uncertain, and agree on the next practical check.

DFEA.name: Explorer
DFEA.summary: Try different tools and let the experience reveal new possibilities.
DFEA.description: You enjoy exploring new possibilities with different tools and often discover what you really want through trying. You are willing to change direction and welcome unexpected discoveries. Beyond whether it works, you want to see what new expression different combinations can create.
DFEA.inPractice: You may try different tools and combinations, then refine the expression around what you discover.
DFEA.watchFor: Interesting possibilities can pull you away from the goal. Separate exploration time from delivery time.
DFEA.collaboration: Share discoveries early and let teammates help choose which direction deserves further work.

DGRU.name: Steward
DGRU.summary: Choose reliable tools and clear rules to make everyday work easier.
DGRU.description: You want to choose reliable tools, arrange the rules and responsibilities, and let things run steadily. You do not want to keep worrying about details the system can handle. You accept some constraints in exchange for fewer surprises, less maintenance, and an easier everyday routine.
DGRU.inPractice: You may choose a suitable platform, define dependable rules, and let it carry routine responsibility.
DGRU.watchFor: Stable defaults still have boundaries. Review them when requirements or dependencies change.
DGRU.collaboration: Clarify who owns each mechanism and make the expected operating rules easy to find.

DGRA.name: Lawmaker
DGRA.summary: Think the rules through and let machines enforce them consistently.
DGRA.description: You believe that once rules are clear, machines should enforce them strictly. Instead of relying on everyone to remember and comply, you prefer types, frameworks, and automated checks to block invalid approaches. You seek consistent order so individual improvisation has less influence on the system.
DGRA.inPractice: You may formalize a model and use established tools to apply its rules consistently.
DGRA.watchFor: Strict rules can make an emerging requirement difficult to express. Check whether the model needs to change.
DGRA.collaboration: Explain the reason for each constraint and provide a clear process for revising the rules.

DGEU.name: Administrator
DGEU.summary: Use proven tools and real observations to keep solving problems reliably.
DGEU.description: You trust mature tools and clear rules, but ultimately judge actual behavior. You use testing and observation to confirm reliability, adjusting configuration or changing the solution when needed. You do not need control over every internal detail; you care about solving problems consistently over time.
DGEU.inPractice: You may verify mature tools against actual needs, then adjust configuration while preserving useful guarantees.
DGEU.watchFor: Observed stability can change under a new workload. Keep representative checks tied to the operating context.
DGEU.collaboration: Share the measurements behind choices and make configuration responsibilities explicit.

DGEA.name: Sound Engineer
DGEA.summary: Try and adjust until every part works in harmony with the others.
DGEA.description: You want mature tools to follow consistent rules and keep adjusting them through use. Each part working on its own is not enough: together, their interfaces should agree, their behavior should feel natural, and their details should not conflict. You seek a system whose parts fit just right.
DGEA.inPractice: You may use mature components and keep testing their interfaces until the combined system feels coherent.
DGEA.watchFor: Aligning every detail may require costly wrappers. Check whether the consistency benefit justifies another layer.
DGEA.collaboration: Show where interfaces disagree and agree on the conventions the whole system should share.

preferencePractice.C: You tend to keep key mechanisms visible and adjustable. In practice, you may prefer explicit wiring, configurable policies, or a locally maintained change when a tool hides important behavior.
preferencePractice.D: You tend to let suitable tools own general mechanisms. Existing modules, supported plugins, and managed build steps can leave you more room for business-specific work.
preferencePractice.F: You tend to retain composition and adjustment freedom. Open data objects, configurable processing, and checks at use sites can suit requirements that are still taking shape.
preferencePractice.G: You tend to encode permitted behavior upfront. Separate result types, constrained API methods, and explicit transitions can make the allowed paths visible in the code.
preferencePractice.R: You tend to build an explanation before choosing the first check. Call chains, cost estimates, and possible execution orders help you decide what evidence to gather.
preferencePractice.E: You tend to gather observations before deep analysis. Reproductions, small prototypes, and measurements help you decide what to investigate next.
preferencePractice.U: You tend to tie extra work to a practical need. New requirements, repeated edits, and migration costs influence when you refactor, extract a helper, or preserve an existing interface.
preferencePractice.A: You tend to value coherent concepts and expression in their own right. Clear responsibilities, precise names, and consistent internal implementations can justify additional effort.

questions.Q01: When two frameworks both meet my needs, I would prefer the one with an inspectable request-handling process, even if setup takes more steps.
questions.Q02: If an API can return success or failure, I would define separate result types so the code restricts the fields each can contain upfront.
questions.Q03: When a function returns an unexpected result, I would read along its call chain to infer where the problem might be before running a check.
questions.Q04: When code passes existing tests and has no evident maintenance problems, I would wait until it gets in the way of implementing a new requirement before considering refactoring.
questions.Q05: When a project must support several databases, I would prefer an existing data-access tool to handle their differences if it meets the requirements.
questions.Q06: In a small script with evolving requirements, I would prefer data objects that can gain fields as needed, with suitability checks when the fields are read.
questions.Q07: When a bug occurs intermittently, I would narrow the inputs and rerun the failing scenario before analyzing its cause.
questions.Q08: When two implementations can deliver the same feature, I would be willing to spend much more time on the one with clearer responsibilities and a more coherent structure.
questions.Q09: Even for a small reusable module, I would prefer a mature open-source library that meets my needs over implementing my own version.
questions.Q10: When writing linked data-processing functions, I would let callers choose the order and check at runtime whether each step can use the previous step’s output.
questions.Q11: If I am unsure which of two algorithms is faster, I would compare them on typical project data before deciding which to investigate further.
questions.Q12: After a feature works and its variable names are understandable, I would still spend time distinguishing the names of variables with similar but different meanings.
questions.Q13: If failed requests need automatic retries, I would prefer to set retry counts and intervals myself, even if a mature tool’s defaults meet the requirements.
questions.Q14: If an API has invocation modes that cannot be combined, I would use separate methods that each accept only the parameters for that mode.
questions.Q15: If a program with repeated loops and data queries slows down, I would estimate loop counts and per-query costs before deciding what to measure.
questions.Q16: For an internal tool used by a few colleagues, I would prefer instructions for their actual use and defer full documentation until its audience grows.
questions.Q17: When one internal behavior prevents a library from meeting my needs, I would be willing to maintain a modified version to control that behavior directly.
questions.Q18: If a task has pending, active, and completed states, I would list allowed transitions upfront and restrict its update method to those transitions.
questions.Q19: If storing API results could reduce repeated queries, I would work out how long to retain them and when updates should clear them before experimenting.
questions.Q20: Even when a business concept appears only once, I would be willing to give it its own class or module so it has a clear place in the code.
questions.Q21: If logs need custom information and an existing logging library’s extension interface supports it, I would use that interface and leave internal processing to the library.
questions.Q22: For a frequently changing experimental feature, I would prefer adjustable configuration options, with their combinations checked when the configuration is read.
questions.Q23: When evaluating a new framework, I would implement a small feature with it before reading the documentation in depth about specific issues.
questions.Q24: When similar code blocks are short and easy to change independently, I would prefer to keep them until repeated edits become burdensome before extracting a shared function.
questions.Q25: If an existing platform can compile, test, and package the code, I would let it arrange and maintain those steps.
questions.Q26: When data checks differ slightly across business contexts, I would prefer each call site to choose its checks and retain room for adjustment.
questions.Q27: When unsure how much data to process per batch, I would try several batch sizes and use timings and failures to identify a workable range.
questions.Q28: When an older API's naming is untidy but users understand it, I would prefer to keep it and avoid requiring callers to rename their usage.
questions.Q29: If a framework can discover and connect modules automatically, I would still state which module depends on which in code, even if that requires additional wiring.
questions.Q30: When adding operating modes to a tool, I would prefer to define allowed configurations for each mode upfront and reject other combinations during configuration checks.
questions.Q31: If two tasks might read and write the same data at the same time, I would sketch execution orders and infer conflict points before testing them.
questions.Q32: In code review, when two internal modules use different but understandable approaches, I would still want to spend time expressing the same logic consistently.
